name: Ulrich Zwingli and the Anabaptists

objectives.text: Identify Ulrich Zwingli as a pastor in Zurich, Switzerland, who taught his church from the Bible
Name the Anabaptists as a group who taught that only people who confess faith should be baptized, which led others to call them rebaptizers
Retell how Zwingli began in 1519 to preach through the Gospel of Matthew verse by verse instead of following the assigned readings
Recount that early Anabaptist leaders such as Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz were punished by both Roman Catholic and Protestant authorities, including the drowning of Manz in Zurich in 1527
Describe the 1522 Affair of the Sausages and explain Zwingli's argument that Scripture does not require Christians to keep the Lenten fast
Describe how the Zurich disputations of 1523 and Zwingli's Sixty-Seven Articles sought to settle church questions by appeal to Scripture
Describe Zwingli's death at the Battle of Kappel in 1531 and Heinrich Bullinger's role in continuing the Zurich reformation
Summarize the disagreement between Luther and Zwingli over the Lord's Supper at the Marburg Colloquy of 1529, including their readings of the words this is my body
Explain the Anabaptist case for believer's baptism from the New Testament passages they cited
Explain how Zwingli reformed worship in Zurich by removing images and simplifying the service on the basis of the second commandment
Compare Zwingli's memorial view of the Lord's Supper with the later Reformed confessional teaching of a spiritual feeding on Christ by faith
Contrast the Magisterial Reformers' view that the civil magistrate should support the true church with the Anabaptist call for a church separate from the state
Explain the Reformed case for infant baptism that Zwingli set against the Anabaptists, grounded in the continuity of God's covenant with believers and their children
Trace how Menno Simons and later movements such as the Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites descend from sixteenth-century Anabaptism
Analyze the seven articles of the Schleitheim Confession of 1527 and the Scripture passages Anabaptists used to support them
Explain why Zurich and other Protestant authorities treated Anabaptism as a threat to civil and religious order and punished its followers
Construct a comparison of Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist teaching on baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the relationship of church and state
Evaluate the Anabaptist rejection of oaths, military service, and civil office in light of Scripture and the Reformed confessional position
Evaluate the Protestant persecution of Anabaptists using biblical teaching on the nature of Christ's kingdom and on living at peace with others
Evaluate the Anabaptist idea of a believers' church against the Reformed teaching that the visible church includes believers and their children
Produce a research study distinguishing the violent Münster Rebellion of 1534 to 1535 from peaceful Anabaptism and analyzing how Münster shaped later views of the movement

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: identifying Zwingli, naming the Anabaptists, the Marburg Colloquy, believer's baptism, Magisterial vs Radical views of church and state (merged with the separation objective), the Affair of the Sausages, Amish and Mennonite descent, the three-tradition comparison, pacifism (widened to oaths and civil office), and the Münster study. Dropped filler: 'obey the Bible exactly', 'persecuted by everyone' (replaced with an accurate account of Grebel and Manz), and 'apply the courage to stand for conviction', which is a disposition rather than an assessable skill. Recast 'defend a Believers' Church' as an evaluation against the Reformed confessional teaching on the visible church, and recast the tragedy of persecution as an explanation of Zurich's reasons plus a biblical evaluation. Added Zwingli's lectio continua preaching, the 1523 disputations and Sixty-Seven Articles, his death at Kappel and Bullinger's succession, worship reform under the second commandment, the Reformed covenantal case for infant baptism, the comparison of Zwingli's memorial view with later Reformed teaching on the Supper, and the Schleitheim Confession. Anchored objectives to specific verses and to WCF, Heidelberg, and Shorter Catechism articles only where they state the doctrine. Questions centered on Calvin, Luther, and the Solas were left to the sibling sub-topics.
